issue_context.title: Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Systemd.SystemdHelpers.IsSystemdService does not work inside containers.
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.UseSystemd()` is set up to no-op if `IsSystemdService()` returns false. However, `IsSystemdService()` only returns true if the direct parent process is systemd. This is not true when we have a container runtime (e.g. podman) acting as a middleman, and thus containerised systemd services do not have sd-notify integration or systemd log formatting. 

### Expected Behavior

If there exists a more robust check that would work in containerised deployments, then `IsSystemdService()` should use that.

Otherwise, an overload of` UseSystemd()` should be created (e.g. `UseSystemd(bool forceEnable = false)`) that allows users to forcibly enable sd-notify integration and systemd log formatting, without having to manually copy the part of `UseSystemd()` that is inside the if statement from the reference source into our startup code, since this code may be subject to change in the future.

### Steps To Reproduce

Minimalist reproduction [here](https://github.com/judilsteve/FdListenTest)

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

6.0.101

> Minimalist reproduction [here](https://github.com/judilsteve/FdListenTest)

It's great when issues are reported with a small reproducer. Thanks!

> If there exists a more robust check that would work in containerised deployments, then IsSystemdService() should use that.

We can extend the logic to include the following:

If `Environment.ProcessId` is `1` and the envvar for `NOTIFY_SOCKET` or `LISTEN_PID` is set.

If we'd like to be more liberal, we could drop the `Environment.ProcessId` check. Though the existing `IsSystemdService` check requires .NET to be a direct child, so requiring the process to be pid `1` in the container is similarly strict.

> Otherwise, an overload of UseSystemd() should be created (e.g. UseSystemd(bool forceEnable = false)) that allows users to forcibly enable sd-notify integration and systemd log formatting, without having to manually copy the part of UseSystemd() that is inside the if statement from the reference source into our startup code, since this code may be subject to change in the future.

If we extend the logic of `IsSystemdService` as described above, probably this is not needed.

In case the api would be extended, it should probably use the 'Options' pattern so the systemd mode can be triggered using the regular configuration mechanism.

@judilsteve do you want to contribute the change?
@tmds I'll see if I can take a run at it tomorrow after work, but I haven't contributed to dotnet before, so I might need some guidance as to the project's style/conventions in the resulting PR.

@tmds I am not sure it's appropriate for `IsSystemdService` to return true if `LISTEN_PID` is defined. It is possible to have this defined but have `NOTIFY_SOCKET` (the thing we're actually interested in) not be defined, e.g. if the application is running as a socket-activated containerised service but docker/podman is configured with `--sdnotify=conmon` instead of `--sdnotify=container`. I will proceed with just checking `Environment.ProcessId` and `NOTIFY_SOCKET` for now.

My suggestion is to return `true` if _either_ `NOTIFY_SOCKET` or `LISTEN_PID` is defined, it doesn't have to be both.
So if you are interested in `NOTIFY_SOCKET` and not `LISTEN_PID`, that will work.

My worry was that we would be enabling the services that interact with sd-notify when no notify socket is available, but that service has [its own check](https://source.dot.net/#Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Systemd/SystemdNotifier.cs,cf1bf77e57d89fdd,references) for that, so we're good there. I also forgot that `UseSystemd()` enables journald log formatting, which users may want even if they're not using sd-notify.

For my learning, what is the scenario/reasoning for running a systemd service inside a container? Why not just be a normal process if you are inside a container?

> For my learning, what is the scenario/reasoning for running a systemd service inside a container? Why not just be a normal process if you are inside a container?

The app is packaged and distributed as a container image.
This systemd service can be running any image, like the redis image from Docker hub, or a .NET app from your companies local container registry.

Because the app is packaged as a container image, it is fully self-contained.

`podman` includes a service (`podman-auto-update`) that will check the registry for new images and rolls them out for you. So your app gets updated automatically.

review_comments:
@eerhardt @judilsteve 

As I mentioned in the corresponding issue, this is a good way to check the current process is main process in the container.

In case we're not pid 1, we could extend it with checking if the pid 1 environment (`/proc/1/environ`) contains a `container` envvar. This file may be inaccessible. That is the way systemd itself checks if it runs as systemd in a container. And systemd sets this for its containerized services.

If we want to be looser, we could drop the checks and just rely on the envvars.

I'm fine with the implementation as is. I want to mention the options.
